title: Why seek the living among the dead? (Luke 24:1–12)
hookLine: the women tell the apostles, who think it idle tales
tomorrow: known in the breaking of bread

cards: Sunday, very early. The sabbath is over. A small group of women set out in the gray light, carrying the spices they prepared, to do the last thing love can do for a body.
They know exactly where the tomb is; they watched Joseph lay him there. They are not expecting anything. When they arrive, the stone is already rolled away.
They go inside. The body isn't there. Luke says they were much perplexed.
And then, suddenly, two men are standing beside them in shining garments.

teach.b: The women are terrified and bow their faces to the ground. And the two men ask a question, in the King James words: "Why seek ye the living among the dead? He is not here, but is risen."
Remember what he told you in Galilee, that the Son of man must be delivered, crucified, and rise again the third day. And they remembered his words.
Notice who's being reminded: these women had been listening all along. They're disciples, and Luke names them: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and other women with them.
They go back and tell the eleven and the rest.
And then: "And their words seemed to them as idle tales, and they believed them not." Idle tales. The Greek word is lēros: nonsense, empty talk.
So in Luke the news of the resurrection comes first from women, and the men dismiss it. Luke doesn't hide it. He tells it plainly, and some readers see that plainness as a mark of honesty.
Then Peter gets up and runs to the tomb anyway.

teach.h: HE IS NOT HERE, BUT IS RISEN.
teach.b: He stoops down, sees the linen cloths lying by themselves, and goes home wondering. Not sure yet. Wondering.

how: Christians celebrate the resurrection every Easter and gather on Sundays because the tomb was found empty on the first day of the week; Orthodox Christians honor the women who came with spices as the Myrrh-bearers.

games.q: you're one of the eleven. some women burst in saying the tomb is empty and he is risen. what do you do?

think it's nonsense and stay put.
games.why: their words seemed to them as idle tales. Peter got up and ran to the tomb anyway, and even he went home wondering.

practice: Think of a time, if there was one, when a woman said something true and wasn't taken seriously, by you or by the people around you: a mother who saw a problem coming, a colleague whose idea went to someone else, a friend told she was overreacting.
Hold that memory honestly, and think of one woman whose word you could take more seriously. If you pray, you can give thanks for her.

wordCard.voice: Leros, the Greek word for nonsense, idle talk: what the apostles called the women's report of the empty tomb, when they came with spices for a body that wasn't there.

orig.note: Greek: nonsense, idle talk. Luke's word for how the women's report sounded to the apostles.

carryVoice: Your line: he is not here. A week from Peter's tears to Herod, Barabbas, the road, the cross, the tomb, and this question. That's day five hundred eighty-eight, and another week on the path.
